definition: A concrete, near-algorithmic rule for finding which frames of a reference clip should become key poses: track the character's center of gravity (COG) as a line/curve across the clip, and treat every LOCAL EXTREME of that line (where it starts, stops, or slows down before reversing direction — an ease-in-turnaround-ease-out point) as a key pose, together with every CONTACT (foot-ground or hand-surface touch) — 'we're looking for extremes in the center of gravity and we're looking for contacts[,] those are the two things I'm looking out for most of the time when finding what poses to use in reference'.
purpose: Give a repeatable, non-arbitrary method for choosing key poses from reference footage, rather than picking poses by eye or by guessing which frames 'look important' — a turning point in the COG's own trajectory is a structural fact about the motion, not a judgment call.
visible_effect: Each chosen key pose corresponds to a real inflection in the tracked COG line (a peak, a trough, or a stall before reversal) or a real ground/surface contact, rather than an arbitrarily-spaced sample.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: not applicable — a pose-selection method, not a viewer-facing effect on its own (though poses chosen this way are more likely to already carry good spacing/timing information, per progressive_spacing_via_pose_density_before_curve_interpolation, video 94, this batch).
physical_interpretation: A COG's trajectory extremum IS the physical moment a body's overall momentum reverses or arrests (the top of a jump's hang, the bottom of a squash) — these are load-bearing instants in real motion, which is why they make structurally correct key poses rather than arbitrary ones.
use_cases: extracting key poses from any reference clip (video or a real performer) by tracking a COG proxy line across it and marking its turning points, then adding ground/surface contacts

distinguishing a true KEY (a COG extreme or a contact) from a mere BREAKDOWN (an in-between pose, even one where a body part like the feet is 'offset' at that moment) — the video explicitly treats a contact whose feet arrive asynchronously as a breakdown rather than a key, driven by the COG line's own shape at that frame
non_use_cases: a shot with no clear COG trajectory to track (a purely facial/acting beat with minimal COG movement) — there, other criteria (holds, acting beats) would need to substitute
interactions: contact_poses_derived_as_breakdowns_between_extremes_not_posed_independently (this same batch, video 99) — the companion technique: once extremes are found this way, contacts between them are generated as biased breakdowns rather than posed from scratch.
cadence_representation: Partially buildable, checked directly against the actual measurement code rather than assumed: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion` already samples an arbitrary part's world position across a frame range (a caller could pass a root/hip part as a COG proxy), and its own velocity/acceleration measurements (Part 23) would show a zero-crossing at exactly the turning points this entry needs — but this session found NO local-extrema/turning-point detector as a named measurement in `ai/motion.js` (grepped directly: no `extrema` or `center_of_mass` trajectory function exists). The raw data this technique needs is already sampled; the specific 'find the turning points' step is not currently a built measurement.
control_surface: `sampleMotion`, pointed at a root/COG-proxy part, would supply the raw trajectory this technique needs.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Buildable today from existing data: a local-extrema finder over `sampleMotion`'s position series (a sign change in velocity) would directly implement this entry's key-pose criterion — not currently built, but not blocked on any missing capability either.
generation_or_modification_methods: not applicable — a reference-analysis technique for choosing WHERE to key, not a generation operation itself.
failure_modes: choosing key poses by eye without reference to the COG's actual trajectory shape, risking keys that do not correspond to real structural turning points in the motion
keying a contact as a full key pose when the body parts arriving at it are actually offset/asynchronous (better treated as a breakdown, per this entry's own distinction)
roblox_considerations: None specific — a reference-analysis technique independent of the target engine.
examples: the presenter's own words, verbatim: 'I'm looking at areas like the center of gravity[,] when it kind of starts and stops and slows down[,] and when we get to these extremes where things ease in[,] turn around[,] and ease back out[,] we're usually looking for the most extreme point[,] that would be usually a key' (transcript 0:57-1:09), and 'we could put the contact as [a] key but the feet are kind of offset from each other[,] so I'm going to kind of treat that more as a breakdown' (transcript 1:57-2:03)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/UkWnwHwMapQ @ 0:44-2:46 — Chester Sampson demonstrates tracking a jump reference clip's COG line and marking its extremes and contacts as keys directly, transcript-only per this video's detail setting; cross-checked in this session against `ai/motion.js sampleMotion` (grepped for an existing extrema/center-of-mass function, found none); experimental until validated
